title: Web
instruction: Build each web page from the system, opening on the reader’s question.
intro: This chapter sets how our website looks and works. It covers the masthead, the menu and the footer every page shares; the home page, an article and an Act page; the preview a link shows when someone shares it; and the icon in a browser tab. Every page is built from the tokens and the components in chapter 18, in the light and the dark theme, at the four widths we test.

The pages here are real. The home page leads with one piece for each pillar: our explainer on special districts; our tracker for H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act, a bill that would limit stock purchases by members of Congress and require photo ID to vote in federal elections; a guide to who sets an electric bill; and a rule open for comment. The Act page walks through commenting on that rule, checked November 21, 2026. Only the web address is a stand-in, labeled Illustrative until our founder and editor settles it.

groups.title: The frame every page shares
groups.line: Every page opens with the same masthead, closes with the same footer, names itself in its title and offers the theme switch in one place.

groups.title: Three pages
groups.line: The home page, an article and an Act page, each at four widths and in the dark theme, built from one set of parts.

groups.title: Beyond the page
groups.line: The preview a shared link shows, and the icons a browser and a phone draw for the site.

rules.title: Open every page with the same masthead, and move its parts behind Menu once they no longer fit in the bar.
rule: Every page opens with the same masthead. From 64em, 1,024 px at the default text size, the bar holds L3, the wordmark with the lockmark, at the left and the seven parts of the site at the right, in this order: Explain, Track, Connect, Act, Who Do They Answer To?, About and Subscribe. The theme switch sits on a row beneath them, at the right edge.

Between 48em and 64em the bar keeps L3 and moves the parts and the switch behind Menu, and under 48em the bar sets L1, the wordmark alone, with Menu beside it. The part the reader is in shows in bold with a 2 px underline. Every part stays in the masthead’s ink, Subscribe included, so the view’s one red stays free for the step a reader can take. On an atlas page, the atlas’s own title bar sits under the masthead.

text: A reader finds the parts in the same place on every page, and a screen reader reaches them as one named set of links. The parts come in the order of the pillars and then the rest, so the list itself says what we do. Once the seven no longer fit beside L3, a Menu button keeps them one press away and leaves the wordmark its room.
why.basis: Rules 03.6, 08.2 and 18.6; the parts approved by our founder and editor on November 21, 2026; design judgment for the breakpoints, from measured word widths

rules.title: Under 64em, open the parts in a menu that holds focus, with the theme switch at its top.
rule: Menu opens the parts of the site in a dialog that covers the page. Its title, Menu, and Close the menu sit at the top, then the theme switch, then the seven parts as rows, with the current part on the selected band.

Focus moves to the current part, or to Close the menu on a page with no current part. Tab and Shift+Tab keep focus inside the menu. Escape or Close the menu closes it and returns focus to Menu, and a part opens its page. If the window widens past 64em while the menu is open, it closes and focus moves to the current part in the bar, or to the home link on a page with none.

text: A dialog makes the page behind it unreachable, so a keyboard or screen reader user never walks into links the menu covers. The switch at the top keeps the theme one press away on a phone, where the bar has no room for it.
why.basis: Rule 18.6 and the Dialog (Modal) pattern in the W3C’s ARIA Authoring Practices Guide; design judgment for the order inside

correct.caption: The menu open over the article page at 390 and 360 px in the light theme and at 390 px in the dark theme, with Explain on the selected band.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 20.2. The menu leaves the theme switch out, so on a phone a reader cannot change the theme from any page.

rules.title: Close every page with the same footer: the parts, help in one place, and the lockmark with the tagline.
rule: Every page ends with the same footer. Four lists name the site again: our work by pillar, the atlas, Oath & Action, and Help, whose one link, Contact us, opens our contact page. Help keeps its place in that order on every page, the atlas’s pages included.
Under the lists, a Charcoal strip closes the page with the lockmark at 24 px and the tagline on one line, and the web address after them.

text: A reader who gets stuck finds help where they found it last time, which matters most on the page where they are trying to take part. The lockmark closes the page in the footer, and since the masthead scrolls away, its lockmark and the footer’s never share a screen (Rule 08.2).
why.basis: Rule 08.2; WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.6, as the W3C’s page “Understanding Success Criterion 3.2.6: Consistent Help”, retrieved November 21, 2026, sets it; the web address shown as a stand-in, approved by our founder and editor on November 21, 2026

correct.caption: The footer at 1440, 1024, 390 and 360 px in the light theme, and at 1440 px in the dark theme, where a hairline edges its Charcoal strip.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 20.3. Help moves and changes its words from one page to the next, so a reader has to hunt for it on the page where they need it most.

rules.title: Name every page in its title, and set its language in the markup.
rule: Give every page a title that starts with its own words and ends with our name, as in “What a special district does | Oath & Action”. The home page leads with our name and the tagline. Set the language of every page on its root, as lang="en".

When a passage or phrase is in another language, mark the smallest element that holds it with its own language, and leave names and terms that English uses as they are, such as Regulations.gov or N-acetyl-L-cysteine.

text: A title is the first thing a screen reader says and the name a tab, a bookmark and a search result show, so a reader with ten tabs open can find this one. The language tells a screen reader how to pronounce the words and tells a browser which characters to draw.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.2, 3.1.1 and 3.1.2, and Technique G88, as the W3C’s pages set them, retrieved November 21, 2026

correct.caption: Three tabs a reader can tell apart, the head every page carries, and a phrase in another language marked with its own.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 20.4. Every tab says Oath & Action, so a reader cannot tell the explainer from the Act page without opening each one.

rules.title: Draw every page in the dark theme from the same markup, and keep each panel’s edge.
rule: Every page follows the reader’s device at first and changes theme from the switch, with no second page and no second set of words. The dark theme sets Charcoal for the page and the matching value for every part.

A dark panel keeps its Charcoal and draws a 1 px edge, so it still reads as a panel on a Charcoal page. Charts take the chart kit’s Charcoal drawing, and the identity marks take their paint for Charcoal.

text: One page in two themes keeps the words, links and order the same for every reader. Without an edge, a Charcoal panel on a Charcoal page disappears, and the section loses the signal that told the reader it had turned.
why.basis: One dark theme for every screen product, with a visible switch that remembers the reader’s choice, approved by our founder and editor on November 10, 2026; Rules 18.4 and 26.6; design judgment for the edge

correct.caption: The home page’s first screen at 390 px in the light and the dark theme, from the same markup. On the dark page each head cell of the pillar row keeps a 1 px edge along its top and foot.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 20.5. With no edge, the pillar cell melts into the dark page, and only its icon and word show where the section begins.

rules.title: Open the home page on one piece for each pillar, with the step a reader can take now.
rule: The home page opens on the pillar row, with one piece under each pillar: an explainer, a tracker, a guide and a step a reader can take now. Each piece is a card with its kicker, headline, a few lines and its date. The Act card carries the take-part mark on its step and the view’s one red.
Below them, the atlas’s section opens on its title bar, then lists the everyday questions it answers beside a chart and its source line.

text: A first-time reader sees in one screen what each pillar does and one thing they can do now. The pillar row is the order of our work, so it can order the page without a word of explanation.
why.basis: Rules 01.21, 09.1, 09.4, 11.4, 11.5 and 11.9; design judgment for the layout

correct.caption: The home page at 1440, 1024, 390 and 360 px in the light theme, and at 1440 and 390 px in the dark theme. At 1,024 px the pillar row breaks after Track, two pillars to a line, as Rule 09.1 sets it.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 20.6. The first screen opens on a slogan, so a reader learns nothing they can use and finds no step to take.

rules.title: Build an article from its question to its step, with the chart whole in its column.
rule: An article opens with the compact pillar row, its kicker and a headline that answers the reader’s question, then an intro of two or three sentences and the byline. Its body runs at the reading measure, and a chart keeps all its parts, its source line and its table in the body’s column.
The last section ends on a step the reader can take, and the last word carries ampersand B.

text: A reader who came with a question gets the answer in the headline and the evidence in the column they are already reading. Ending on a step tells them what to do with what they learned.
why.basis: Rules 01.21, 02.8, 04.6, 07.3, 09.1 and 14.2; the counts from the Census Bureau’s 2022 Census of Governments

correct.caption: The article at 1440, 1024, 390 and 360 px in the light theme, and at 1440 and 390 px in the dark theme. The count panel is the first screen’s one dark panel.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 20.7. The article ends on a slogan, so a reader who wants to see which districts their state has finishes with nowhere to go.

rules.title: Build an Act page as a process piece that names who decides and by when, with one way to take part in red.
rule: An Act page opens on the step and its date: what the agency proposes, who decides and when comments close, with the rule’s steps beside the opening and the ask under the step that is open. It quotes the agency’s own summary, sets out what the record shows from those who asked for the change and on the concern the law guards, at the length the record holds, and takes no side.

After the hinge divider it lists how to comment, online and by mail, what becomes public and how to read other comments, and gives the ask again. The ask is a red link to the comment page that names the action and the place, with the docket number beside it, and the page says the day we checked its facts.

text: A reader of any view can use the page, because it tells them how to be heard and leaves what to say to them. Naming the place in the link tells a reader they are leaving our site before they press it.
why.basis: Rules 01.22, 04.4, 11.4, 11.6, 11.9 and 11.15; the docket as the Federal Register and govinfo.gov printed it, retrieved November 21, 2026; the page’s subject approved by our founder and editor on November 21, 2026

correct.caption: The Act page at 1440, 1024, 390 and 360 px in the light theme, and at 1440 and 390 px in the dark theme. Its red does one job, the step: the take-part mark with the ask under it, and the ask again after the instructions.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 20.8. “Take action” names no place, so a reader cannot tell where the link leads or that it leaves our site.

rules.title: Give each section one dark panel in its opening screen, and let running text stay Newsprint.
rule: Measure a long page one screen at a time. The first screen and each section’s opening screen hold 60 to 85 percent Newsprint and at most one dark panel, and Pillar Red stays within 5 percent.
Put each section’s dark panel where its opening screen needs it, and let the screens of running text between them hold more Newsprint.

text: A reader judges a page one screen at a time. A dark panel at the turn of each section tells them something new begins, and long stretches of reading stay calm on Newsprint.
why.basis: Rule 05.1, with its sentence for long pages approved by our founder and editor on November 21, 2026; the application kit’s measure of each screen

correct.caption: Every first and opening screen of the three pages at 1440 px in the light theme, measured on the application kit’s captures.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 20.9. With no panel in its first screen, our studio sample of this article measured 88.2 percent Newsprint, past the 85 a screen allows.

rules.title: Share every page as a 1200 by 630 card, its headline over a Charcoal foot that holds the sign-off.
rule: Each page shares as a 1200 by 630 card on Newsprint: the page’s kicker in the H3 style, its headline at the title size, and a Charcoal foot that holds the wordmark at the left and the lockmark’s 96 px sign-off at the right.
The card carries no web address until ours is settled, no deck and no icon, and its words go into the image’s alt text too.

text: A feed shows the card at about 500 px wide, so only the headline and the marks survive, and the sign-off at 96 px keeps its lever red at that size. The foot puts the card in Rule 05.1’s range and gives every shared page the same signature in the same place.
why.basis: Rule 08.2 and its feed test; the link-preview card in the identity proofs; the platform rows retrieved November 21, 2026; design judgment for the foot

correct.caption: The article’s share preview at full size and at the two widths a feed shows it.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 20.10. At 48 px the sign-off loses its lever’s red once a feed shrinks the card to 360 px; Rule 08.2 counted no red pixel left on our card.
